name: Snoring mouthpiece (Anti-snore mouthpiece)

card.summary: An oral device worn at night that holds the lower jaw slightly forward to keep the airway open, used by people who want quieter, more consolidated sleep and the fresher, less puffy look that goes with it.
card.aka: Anti-snore mouthpiece, mandibular advancement device, boil-and-bite mouthguard, ZQuiet-style devices
card.note: Jaw and tooth discomfort and bite changes are reported; snoring can be a sign of sleep apnea that warrants a medical evaluation.

quick.overview:
A snoring mouthpiece is a mouthguard-style device worn during sleep that moves the lower jaw (and with it the tongue base) slightly forward. This widens the space at the back of the throat so the airway vibrates and collapses less. People use it to reduce snoring and to sleep more continuously, and better sleep is associated with a rested face, steadier energy for training and fewer dark circles.

The category has a research base: clinical sleep-medicine guidelines support custom-made mandibular advancement devices for primary snoring and for some people with sleep apnea. Over-the-counter thermoplastic versions are a cheaper variant whose performance has been studied less favourably. In forum culture, the device appears mostly in lifters' sleep and recovery threads rather than as a facial-structure tool.
quick.how: Over-the-counter models are typically softened in hot water and bitten into to take an impression of the teeth; custom models are made by a dentist from a scan or mold of the mouth. The device is worn each night, and users describe an adjustment period of several nights to weeks. Some people combine it with side-sleeping, nasal strips or weight management; others are using it as a substitute or alternative for CPAP.
quick.risks: Commonly reported effects are dry mouth, tooth or jaw soreness and excess salivation. Longer-term use has been associated with small shifts in how the teeth meet. Many users stop because of discomfort. Because loud snoring can accompany obstructive sleep apnea, clinicians generally recommend that a sleep evaluation guide the choice of device.

lead: A snoring mouthpiece, also sold as an anti-snore mouthpiece or mandibular advancement device (MAD), is an oral appliance worn during sleep that holds the lower jaw slightly forward. By tightening the soft tissues and muscles of the upper airway, it reduces the vibration that causes snoring and the airway collapse seen in some sleep-disordered breathing.[1]

People use it to look better through sleep. Uninterrupted sleep is associated with a rested appearance, and in lifting communities snoring and poor sleep are discussed as obstacles to recovery and training. On T Nation, members describe buying over-the-counter devices after sleep studies or on a spouse's suggestion, with one reporting that they tried a ZQuiet mouthpiece after waking repeatedly tired and sore.[2][3]

Custom-made devices are supported by American Academy of Sleep Medicine and American Academy of Dental Sleep Medicine guidance for primary snoring and for people with sleep apnea who cannot tolerate CPAP, according to Wikipedia's summary. Over-the-counter thermoplastic models have been judged less favourably in a 2008 study cited there.[1]

chain: Holds the lower jaw forward during sleep
Opens the airway and reduces snoring
Better recovery, energy and a more rested appearance
angle.text: The device acts on the airway, not on the face. Users wear it to sleep more continuously, which they link to better recovery, training and a fresher look in the morning.

infobox: Up to about $1,900 for custom devices (out of pocket)[1]

paras: The device fits over the upper and lower teeth and positions the lower jaw forward. Custom-made versions are produced from a dental impression or scan, and some are 3D-printed with channels for mouth breathing. Thermoplastic over-the-counter versions are shaped by the user, and cheaper non-prescription devices are described in medical references as unproven and potentially problematic.[1]

Moving the mandible forward pulls the tongue base and soft palate structures away from the back of the throat and tightens the muscles of the upper airway. This is intended to limit the collapse and fluttering that produce snoring.[1]

Forum use is mostly practical. T Nation members discussing sleep apnea and snoring describe testing mouthpieces as an alternative to a CPAP machine recommended by a doctor, or after a sleep study showed mild sleep-disordered breathing.[2][4] One member wrote that after ten days with a ZQuiet device they were sleeping through the night.[3] These are individual reports and the experiences vary.

Because the device holds the jaw forward, it is occasionally mentioned alongside jaw-posture topics. Proponents of such practices have not published evidence that a sleep appliance changes facial structure.

Wikipedia's summary of the literature notes that guidelines support oral appliances for primary snoring and for patients who cannot tolerate CPAP, that they work better in mild and moderate than severe sleep apnea, and that a meta-analysis of 51 randomized trials found blood-pressure reductions comparable to CPAP.[1] A 2024 meta-analysis cited there estimated roughly a 66 percent reduction in the apnea-hypopnea index in severe cases.[1]

Common issues are dry mouth, tooth pain, dental discomfort and jaw pain, and many people discontinue because of discomfort, lack of benefit or a switch to CPAP. Long-term use was not linked to temporomandibular disorder in the review summarised, but was associated with lasting changes in how the teeth meet and with periodic repairs or relines.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, mouthpieces come up in sleep apnea and recovery threads as alternatives or add-ons to a prescribed CPAP.[2][4]

claims.claim: A cheap boil-and-bite mouthpiece stopped my snoring and improved my sleep
claims.believers: Some forum members report sleeping through the night within days of starting an over-the-counter device.[3]
claims.experts: Guidelines favour custom dental devices; a 2008 study cited by Wikipedia did not recommend thermoplastic over-the-counter devices as a treatment or screening tool.[1]

claims.claim: A mouthpiece can replace CPAP for sleep apnea
claims.believers: Members who dislike CPAP describe trying a mouthpiece after a doctor advised CPAP.[2]
claims.experts: Oral appliances are supported for people who cannot tolerate CPAP and work better in mild to moderate apnea; they may reduce apnea without eliminating it.[1]
